sections.html:
In the far northwest of South Carolina, against the North Carolina border, Spartanburg County covers 819.74 square miles, with 808.34 of them land. Its seat and largest community is the city of Spartanburg. Greer, Duncan, Boiling Springs, Inman, Landrum and Woodruff ring the city, which means a seller might hold a downtown bungalow, a house in a subdivision off the interstate, or a rural lot.

Millage is decided locally every year, so ask about your own parcel rather than borrowing a neighbor's bill. The older neighborhoods, including Hampton Heights and the Beaumont Mill village, take in a designated local historic district. Owners there should phone the city before planning work on the outside of the house.

Damp, hot summers and 50 to 51 inches of rain annually wear on roofs, gutters and crawl spaces. When repairs have been put off for years, selling as-is can beat paying for all of them first.

Valuation and appeals belong to the Assessor, while collection is split between the Treasurer and the Delinquent Tax Office. Walk in at the Administration Building, 366 N Church Street, Spartanburg, Monday to Friday between 8 AM and 5 PM. Delinquent taxes are handled at 864-596-2597 or P.O. Box 3060, Spartanburg, SC 29304.

Bring your parcel number and your latest notice to any visit. Staff can tell you which office holds the file on your property, and a few minutes at the counter often clears up a question that would take days by letter.

Bills come due anywhere from September 30 to January 15 following the assessment. Late charges stack up in three steps under the county's rules and S.C. Code 12-45-180.

If the bill is unpaid byPenalty addedRunning total
January 163%3%
February 27%10%
March 175%15%

Once March 17 arrives the bill is delinquent and the Treasurer sends a tax execution to the Tax Collector. The Treasurer may waive penalties for a taxpayer who offers clear and convincing evidence of paying on time, and the law covers waivers too when a change of title left the new owner without notice in time.

The latest reappraisal reset values to market conditions on December 31, 2022, and the 2023 bills used those numbers. More than 180,567 notices went into the mail by September 2023.

  • A reappraisal can lift your value by at most 15%, except for new or improved structures, a sale or a transfer of interest.
  • The notice itself is not a bill.
  • The state requires a reappraisal every five years. The Assessor knows the date of the next.

A buyer shouldn't assume the seller's old bill carries over. If the property just sold, the cap may not protect the new owner, so a buyer should work from the new value.

Your objection must be in writing and reach the Assessor within 90 days of the mailing date on the notice. From there the process has five stages.

  1. Ask in writing for a meeting. If the Assessor agrees with you, the value is changed and the matter ends.
  2. Otherwise go to the conference. Skipping it forfeits any further appeal for that year.
  3. Submit a written protest listing your facts, your legal reasons and the value you claim.
  4. The Assessor replies in writing in about 30 days, and you then have 30 days to take it to the County Board of Assessment Appeals.
  5. Within 30 days of the Board's decision, ask for a contested case at the Administrative Law Court.

With no reappraisal notice in a given year, timing decides which year you affect: file before January 15 and it applies to that tax year, file on or after and it applies to the next. Appealing never postpones the payment deadline. Before December 31 you can ask in writing to be billed on at least 80% of the protested value while the case is pending. Evidence from comparable market sales helps; forced, distressed and foreclosure sales generally don't.

Collection escalates in stages: an execution notice, then a notice of seizure, then a public auction. When 30 days pass after the execution notice with no payment, the notice of seizure goes by certified, restricted delivery mail. The property is then advertised weekly for three consecutive weeks before it is sold.

Redemption is open for 12 months to the owner, a grantee of the owner, and a mortgage or judgment creditor. Interest is charged on the bid at 3% for months one to three, 6% for months four to six, 9% for months seven to nine and 12% for months ten to twelve. Without a redemption, the Tax Collector issues a tax deed, which carries no warranty and passes only the county's interest. A top bidder who doesn't pay owes $500 per property.

Under 12-51-120, the owner must get a certified mailing 45 to 20 days ahead of the redemption deadline.

sections.h2: What to bring and what to expect
sections.html:
Bring the tax bill, the parcel number, any execution notice and a photo ID when you visit an office. If the property is inherited, add whatever shows who has authority to sign. For an appeal, add recent sales of similar homes nearby, since comparable market sales count as evidence. Keep a copy of every paper you file, along with the date.

Expect a few steps, not one. The Treasurer quotes the payoff, the closing attorney or title company checks the record, and the deed is recorded after funds move. Setting aside a few days for each step keeps the schedule realistic.

At closing the unpaid balance, including penalties, normally comes out of the seller's proceeds. Under 12-45-140 the county auditor can apportion tax on a transfer, so the closing attorney can tell you how the current year was divided.

  • Obtain the tax bill and any execution notice before you list or take an offer.
  • Request a payoff from the Treasurer that includes penalties.
  • If the bill went to a former owner, ask about a waiver under 12-45-180.
  • Warn a cash buyer from the start if a tax sale clock is ticking.

We purchase Spartanburg County houses in any condition, including ones with back taxes. Send the address and the tax situation, and we will say whether it fits.

A cash sale can be quicker than a listing when a deadline is near, because it doesn't wait on a buyer's lender or an appraisal. Compare the written offer with what a listing might net after repairs, penalties and the weeks of waiting, then choose.

faqs.q: When are Spartanburg County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The window runs September 30 to January 15. After that a 3% penalty starts January 16, 7% more is added on February 2, and 5% more on March 17, reaching 15%.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Spartanburg County assessment?
faqs.a: Within 90 days after the Assessor mails the notice, in writing. Appealing doesn't move your tax due date.

faqs.q: Can I get my Spartanburg County house back after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, within 12 months of the sale. Redeeming means paying taxes, penalties and costs plus interest of 3%, 6%, 9% or 12%, based on the month. A grantee or a mortgage or judgment creditor may also redeem.

faqs.q: Will the 15% reappraisal cap apply after I sell?
faqs.a: Often not. Sold property, an assessable transfer or new or improved structures fall outside the cap, so the buyer's bill follows the new value.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Spartanburg County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is typically cleared from your proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff with penalties, and warn any buyer when a tax sale is close.
